title: Two-Variable Data, Part 3: Traps and the Fast Way

beats.say: In this video, we look at five mistakes students make with two-variable data, and then use Desmos regressions to find a linear model and an exponential model from a table.
Each trap is shown as a wrong line first, then the right line, with the reason it is so tempting.
Trap one. A residual is the actual value minus the predicted value. Reversing the order gives the right size but the wrong sign.
Subtract in the right order. Actual minus predicted is forty-four point five minus forty-eight, which is negative three point five.

scenes.title: Trap 2: a prediction is not certain

beats.say: Trap two. A line of best fit gives an estimate. Answer choices that say will or exactly are usually wrong.
The correct wording is that sales are predicted to be about sixty-five drinks, since individual days vary around the line.

scenes.title: Trap 3: slope is not a total

beats.say: Trap three. In d equals three point two t plus seven, the number three point two is a rate. Students read it as the total amount of growth.
The slope is the predicted change in d per one unit of t. If t is in days, d grows by three point two each day.
beats.right_why: Change per one unit of t

beats.say: Trap four. The values five, fifteen, forty-five, one hundred thirty-five rise quickly, and the first few might look close to a line.
Check the ratios as well as the differences. Every ratio is three, so the data is exponential, with the model five times three to the x.
Trap five. A strong pattern in a scatterplot does not show that changing x causes y to change.
A strong association only shows that the variables move together. A cause needs an experiment, or other evidence, beyond the scatterplot.
Desmos regressions answer which equation fits the data directly. Enter the table, type a tilde, and match the reported constants to the answer choices.
Our first example is the café data. Six temperatures from ten to thirty-five degrees, with the hot-drink sales for each.
Open a fresh graph. We will enter the six data points as a table.
Create a table with the temperatures in the first column and the sales in the second. Each row becomes a point on the graph.
Type y sub one, a tilde, then m times x sub one plus b. Press the right arrow after each subscript.
Desmos reports a slope of about negative two point five five, and an intercept of about one hundred forty-two. That is close to the given line, negative two point five x plus one hundred forty.
For exponential data, type a times b to the x instead. Our data is x equals zero to three, and y equals five, fifteen, forty-five, one hundred thirty-five.
Again we enter the table, and then ask Desmos for the best fitting exponential.
Create a table with the four x values and the four y values. The points curve upward.
Type y sub one, a tilde, then a b to the x sub one. Press the right arrow to leave the subscript, and again to leave the exponent.
Desmos reports a equals five and b equals three. So the model is y equals five times three to the x, matching our work by hand.

Now a practice problem. The line of best fit is y equals negative two point five x plus one hundred forty. A data point is twenty comma ninety-two. Find the residual. Pause the video, try it, and then watch the solution.
First predict y at x equals twenty by substituting into the line, keeping the parentheses around twenty.
Negative two point five times twenty is negative fifty. So the equation becomes negative fifty plus one hundred forty.
Negative fifty plus one hundred forty is ninety. So the line predicts ninety drinks at twenty degrees.
The residual is the actual value minus the predicted value. The actual value is ninety-two, and the prediction is ninety.
Ninety-two minus ninety is two. The positive sign means that the point lies two units above the line.
To recap. A residual is actual minus predicted, a prediction is an estimate, and the slope is a rate per one unit of x.
Check differences and ratios to choose linear or exponential, and remember that association does not prove cause.
Use Desmos regressions to read the constants. In the next topic, we study probability.
